1.title: Human Review, Confidence and Provenance
1.text: Welcome to Module fourteen: Human Review, Confidence and Provenance. This module covers task statements five point five and five point six: human review, confidence and provenance. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. Why an overall accuracy figure can hide weak spots. Stratified random sampling and field-level confidence calibrated on a labeled validation set. Routing documents to human reviewers when capacity is limited. Claim-source mappings, conflicting values, dates and fitting the format to the content.

1.title: Case Check-In: Birchwood Supply Automates Invoice Entry
1.text: Our running case is Birchwood Supply. Birchwood Supply Automates Invoice Entry. The extraction system reports ninety-seven percent accuracy overall, so management wants to stop most human review. Closer inspection shows handwritten receipts at only seventy percent and the tax-I D field often wrong. Reviewers can check only a few hundred documents a week.

1.title: Human Review and Confidence Calibration
1.text: Human Review and Confidence Calibration. Aggregate accuracy hides problems. ninety-seven percent overall can mask poor performance on specific document types or fields. Validate by segment. Measure accuracy by document type and by field before automating high-confidence extractions or reducing review. Stratified random sampling. Keep sampling high-confidence extractions from each segment: it measures the true error rate and detects novel error patterns. Field-level confidence. Have the model output a confidence per field, then calibrate thresholds on a labeled validation set (compare confidence to real correctness). Routing. Send low-confidence, ambiguous or contradictory-source extractions to people; prioritize limited reviewer capacity where errors are most likely.

1.title: Human Review and Confidence Calibration, continued
1.text: Human Review and Confidence Calibration, continued. The figure shows this: Human review design: auto-accept high confidence, but keep a stratified random sample by document type; route low confidence and contradictions to reviewers; use the results to recalibrate. Why sampling the confident ones matters: a threshold chosen once can drift as documents change; random samples show it. Raw model confidence is not a calibrated probability. It becomes useful only after you compare it with ground truth on labeled data and set thresholds from that. Exam tip: "Accuracy is ninety-seven percent, so reduce review" to check accuracy per document type and field first, and keep stratified sampling. Exam tip: Confidence scores are useful only after calibration on a labeled validation set.

1.title: Provenance and Uncertainty in Multi-Source Synthesis
1.text: Provenance and Uncertainty in Multi-Source Synthesis. Case (continued): Birchwood's research system reports two market-size figures: four point one billion dollars from an industry association (two thousand twenty-two data) and five point three billion dollars from an analyst firm (two thousand twenty-five data). The first draft report quietly uses five point three billion dollars and drops the other.

1.title: Provenance and Uncertainty in Multi-Source Synthesis, continued
1.text: Provenance and Uncertainty in Multi-Source Synthesis, continued. Source attribution is lost when findings are compressed in summaries. Require structured claim-source mappings (claim, source U R L (uniform resource locator), document name, relevant excerpt) that the synthesis agent preserves and merges. Conflicting statistics from credible sources. Annotate the conflict with source attribution; do not arbitrarily pick one. Let the coordinator decide how to reconcile. Dates ignored. Require publication or data-collection dates in structured outputs, so a temporal difference of years is not misinterpreted as a contradiction. Everything in one format. Render each content type appropriately: financial data as tables, news as prose, technical findings as structured lists.

1.title: Provenance and Uncertainty in Multi-Source Synthesis, continued
1.text: Provenance and Uncertainty in Multi-Source Synthesis, continued. Established versus disputed claims blended. Use explicit sections that separate well-established findings from contested ones, keeping the original source characterizations and methodological context.

1.title: Provenance and Uncertainty in Multi-Source Synthesis, continued
1.text: Provenance and Uncertainty in Multi-Source Synthesis, continued. The figure shows this: Provenance: every claim travels with its source, excerpt and date; conflicting values are kept side by side and annotated. The document analysis subagent should finish its work with the conflicting values included and annotated and pass them on, rather than resolving the conflict silently. Exam tip: Two credible sources disagree to keep both with attribution (and dates); never "pick the most recent" or "average them" without a stated basis.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Aggregate accuracy: Can hide poor document types or fields to validate by segment first. Sampling: Stratified random samples of high-confidence output to true error rate, novel patterns. Confidence: Field-level; calibrate on a labeled validation set. Routing: Low confidence, ambiguity, contradictions to people; prioritize limited capacity. Provenance: Claim-source mappings (U R L, document, excerpt) preserved through synthesis. Conflicts: Keep both values with attribution; coordinator decides; never pick arbitrarily. Dates: Require publication or collection dates (time differences are not contradictions). Rendering: Finance to tables, news to prose, technical findings to structured lists; separate established from contested.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Invoice extraction shows ninety-seven percent accuracy overall, and management wants to remove most human review. What should the team do first? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Aggregate accuracy can hide weak segments; validate per type and field first.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. How can a team keep detecting new error patterns in extractions that the model rates as high confidence? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Sampling across segments measures error rates and uncovers novel failure patterns.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. Model-reported field confidence scores exist, but nobody knows what "zero point eight five" means in practice. How should review thresholds be set? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Calibration against labeled ground truth turns raw scores into useful routing thresholds.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Reviewer capacity is limited. Which routing rule is best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Concentrate scarce attention on the items most likely to be wrong.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Two reputable sources give different market sizes, one with two thousand twenty-two data and one with two thousand twenty-five data. What should the report do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Preserve both values with attribution and dates; the dates may explain the difference.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. Select two. Which two steps are needed before reducing human review of automated extraction? The five options are on the screen. The answers are D and E. Segment-level accuracy and ongoing sampling show where the system is weak. An overall number can hide poor segments.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. Select two. Which two practices handle conflicting statistics from credible sources correctly? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and B. Both values with attribution and dates let readers judge; the dates may explain the difference.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all seven answers. Question one: C. Question two: A. Question three: C. Question four: B. Question five: A. Question six: D and E. Question seven: A and B. In the next module, we continue the course.
